candidates.title: There's an impostor hiding in the Hyades star cluster. Can you spot it?
candidates.raw_excerpt: For years I looked at Taurus and saw something perfectly sensible. There was the Hyades, the big V-shaped cluster that forms the bull's face, with Aldebaran, noticeably brighter and more orange than the other stars, the dominant star. Every diagram reinforced the arrangement — Aldebaran was the eye of Taurus, the Hyades made the face, and in my head they became one object. Then I discovered that Aldebaran has nothing to do with the Hyades. I remember going outside afterward and looking again, half expecting the deception to become obvious now that I knew. It didn't. Aldebaran still looked completely at home among the other stars . The difference is hidden in the one dimension our eyes judge poorly when we look into space — depth. Aldebaran is about 65 light-years away, while the Hyades are roughly 150 light-years distant. The orange eye of Taurus is a foreground star that happens to lie almost exactly along our line of sight toward the Hyades. This fact exposes one of the most convincing tricks in stargazing. The night sky looks flat, and our brains are extremely willing to believe it. But it has incredible depth — and when you can see parts of the night sky in 3D, that's when you begin to appreciate that you're not looking at a flat map. Instead, you begin to see our cosmic neighborhood as it really is. By appreciating depth, you learn its geography. Once it's dark, look east for a small, tight knot of stars — the Pleiades open cluster (M45) — and then look nearby for a much larger V-shaped arrangement. candidates.raw_excerpt: An independent team of researchers has validated the first image of a supermassive black hole captured by humanity. That, in turn, verifies Einstein's greatest theory, general relativity , which first predicted the existence of black holes and what their immediate surroundings would look like. Captured by a global network of telescopes forming an interferometer called the Event Horizon Telescope (EHT) and revealed to the public in 2019, the image shows the supermassive black hole at the heart of the galaxy Messier 87 (M87), located 55 million light-years away. The image of this black hole , designated M87*, with a mass around 6.5 billion times that of the sun, was an immense scientific achievement. That may lead to the question: why did it need verifying at all? Team leader and researcher with Australia's Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), Samuel Lai explained why capturing the image of a distant black hole is so tricky. "It is like standing in your backyard and trying to take a photo of a doughnut on the moon," Lai said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. Lai and his small Australian team developed advanced machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques to capture information about the black hole's structure and filter out interference resulting from the fact that the EHT was viewing M87* from within our planet's atmosphere. The machine-learning technique called GenDIReCT also accounted for biases introduced by combining telescopes to create an Earth-sized interferometer. "When we applied it to the original EHT dataset, we found a black hole almost identical in size and shape as the historic EHT image. Importantly, our model had no idea what a black hole looked like when we applied it to the M87 data," Lai continued. "This is the first truly independent validation of the EHT image, an important step in the scientific process." candidates.raw_excerpt: PASADENA, Calif. – NASA's Voyager mission team cheered and wiped away tears here on Thursday (Nov. 19), celebrating a big milestone — Voyager 1 just reached one light-day from Earth , something no other spacecraft has ever done. The excitement persisted despite a communication anomaly that cropped up on the probe, which the team remains confident is temporary. Voyager team members gathered for a press conference about the mission at the Von Karman auditorium here at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) — the first such Voyager event since 1989, when Voyager 1's twin, Voyager 2 , flew past Neptune. The gathering served to celebrate Voyager 1 's distance milestone: At 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT) on Wednesday (Nov. 18), the probe reached one light-day from Earth — the distance a photon travels in one day, which is about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers). That means it now takes a full day for a signal to travel from Earth to Voyager 1, the farthest human-made object out in space. "I remember in 1977 I was standing at the Cape watching Voyager launch, and I never thought I would be here today, 49 years later, to celebrate Voyager's one light-day. What an incredible milestone," Voyager project scientist Linda Spilker said during Thursday's event. An unexpected, but manageable, anomaly While this day and this week have been chock-full of excitement over the distance milestone, the Voyager mission team has been hard at work, as usual, keeping the two nearly 50-year-old spacecraft alive and functioning. Unfortunately, as JPL spokesperson Raquel Villanueva shared at this celebration, on Saturday (Nov. 14), Voyager 1 stopped transmitting science and engineering data. The team has remained in contact with Voyager 1 while investigating the issue, and they are confident that they'll be able to solve it soon. candidates.raw_excerpt: The hacks just keep on coming. Days after a major breach of websites belonging to some of the world’s top companies and organizations, data belonging to thousands of credit card users has been leaked by a ransomware group. According to the Wall Street Journal , the data comes from a blend of customers from Visa, Mastercard, and JPMorgan Chase, though it was obtained through an exploit of third-party service platforms. Spokespeople for the companies said the breach encompasses marketing data like names and email addresses, and denied that payment information was obtained as part of the hack. The financial firms also denied that the breach was related to the previous cybersecurity incidents earlier this week. “There is no connection to service disruption of some customers experienced earlier this week,” as JPMorgan Chase told the WSJ . The ransomware group n0n claimed responsibility for the breach. According to cybersecurity firm ZeroFox Intelligence , n0n is a hacking collective that often uses a technique known as double extortion, where hackers essentially demand a ransom from victims both to unlock existing files and stop stolen data from being leaked further. N0n is a new player, with its first appearance coming in September of this year, per ZeroFox. Since then, the collective has conducted an average of two cyberattacks per day, putting it among the cybersecurity firm’s list of “top five most active threat actors globally.” It’s already been an exhausting week of outages, cyberattacks, and tech disruptions — and if this latest incident is any indication, we’re not out of the woods yet. Today (Nov. 18) at 5:16 a.m. EST (1016 GMT), NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft hit one light-day from Earth. About 16 billion miles (about 26 billion kilometers) away, this is the point at which it takes a full day (or 24 hours) for one light particle to get from us to the probe. So any signal we send to Voyager 1 or it sends back now takes a full day as the spacecraft continues to explore interstellar space. To celebrate the major milestone for the farthest human-made object in history, the Empire State Building in New York City lit up in gold . This golden glow references the Golden Record onboard both the Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft. And the Empire State Building wasn't the only major landmark to celebrate the occasion. candidates.raw_excerpt: More than a billion years of Earth's history has seemingly vanished. Now, researchers believe they may have found an explanation, and the answer lies deep inside Earth . Normally, layers of sediment build up over time, eventually forming sedimentary rocks that preserve clues about our planet's past. Older layers generally lie beneath younger ones, allowing geologists to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years. But the geological record isn't always so neatly arranged. In the Grand Canyon, rock layers separated by hundreds of millions of years sit directly on top of one another, revealing a vast gap in Earth's geological record. This enormous gap in Earth's geological timeline is part of the phenomenon known as the Great Unconformity. It's not just the Grand Canyon. Similar gaps have been identified across Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia. Depending on the location, the missing interval ranges from approximately 200 million years to more than a billion years. "Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out," study lead author Santosh Dhungana said in a statement . "The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. candidates.raw_excerpt: AI’s ability to churn out code and find vulnerabilities is making swiss cheese out of the world’s digital infrastructure. On Tuesday, the cybersecurity firm Calif revealed that it used a new OpenAI model to discover a critical flaw in Java, one of the most widely used programming languages in the world which undergirds a vast portion of the online and financial worlds. It’s an eerie example of how the tech is capable of breaching government and corporate systems , at a pace that may soon outstrip our ability to protect those assets — if it hasn’t already. The bug, which the researchers are calling Java4Shell, was discovered in Java’s base64 decoder, a system that allows binary data to be represented as legible plain text. They found that Java bugs out when it tries to decode 64 “A” characters punctuated with a single equal sign. This makes it erroneously execute code, which would normally cause the program to crash by overloading the system’s memory. But using OpenAI’s new GPT-6 cyber model, the researchers found that they could manipulate how the memory is corrupted to access the underlying system and allow a hacker to uncover sensitive data or remotely execute code. Alarmingly, it took little effort to find. Calif says the researcher behind the discovery spent only an hour to uncover the bug, two hours to develop an exploit, and burned less than $200 in AI tokens. Java is an all-around popular programming language, but it’s particularly prevalent among tech, corporate, and government systems. About 90 percent of Fortune 500 companies use it, the N ew York Times noted in its reporting . Perhaps the most alarming find was that the bug could be used to break into Keycloak, a popular open source authentication system used by big organizations ranging from NASA to UnitedHealthcare. “Java is the beating heart of the modern economy,” Bruce Dang, a senior researcher at Calif, told the NYT . “Practically speaking, all major companies” will be affected by the bug, he added.

At that moment the probe was about 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from Earth, the distance light travels in 24 hours. A radio command sent from NASA’s Deep Space Network now takes a full day to reach the spacecraft, and its reply takes another day to come home.
